answer:
Set up the classic 2D dam-break simulation for OpenFOAM (Foundation v10 or later) using the interFoam solver.
Use the standard tutorial dimensions: domain 0.4 m (x) by 0.4 m (y) by 0.01 m (z), with the water column occupying the left portion from x=0 to x=0.1 and spanning the full height y=0 to y=0.4.
Create the mesh with blockMesh as a 2D extrusion: 40 cells in x, 40 cells in y, 1 cell in z, giving a uniform 0.01 m cell size in the x-y plane.
Set the front and back patch boundaries in the z-direction to type empty (2D extrusion).
Set the remaining four patches to type wall with a simple no-slip or slip condition as per the standard damBreak tutorial.
In system/controlDict, set the application line to interFoam.
Configure a simulation time of approximately 0.3 s, with a small deltaT (e.g., 0.0005 s) and adjustable runTime with maxCo around 0.1 for the alphaCourantNo constraint.
Write output every 0.01 s or similar so the free-surface collapse is captured clearly.
In constant/transportProperties, define two incompressible phases: water (rho approximately 1000 kg/m3, nu approximately 1e-6 m2/s) and air (rho approximately 1 kg/m3, nu approximately 1.5e-5 m2/s).
In constant/g, set gravitational acceleration as (0 -9.81 0) for the 2D x-y plane.
Create a setFieldsDict file in system/ with a single boxToCell region specifying min (0 0 0) and max (0.1 0.4 0.01), setting alpha.water to 1 inside the box.
Ensure the default value of alpha.water in the setFieldsDict is 0 so the rest of the domain is filled with air.
Before running setFields, create the initial field file 0/alpha.water with default value uniform 0 and appropriate boundary conditions (zeroGradient on walls).
Create corresponding 0/ and 0.orig/ directories with standard interFoam fields: p_rgh, U, alpha.water, phi.
Execute setFields after mesh creation and field copying so that alpha.water is overwritten to 1 inside the column box and remains 0 elsewhere.
Run the case with interFoam, confirming that the alpha.water field shows a sharp interface (values 0 and 1) collapsing under gravity toward the right side of the domain.
